title: God, the Source of All Good

sections.heading: Seeing that everything comes from you
sections.text: Lord God, you are not small, temporary, or contained by anything you made. The skies show your glory, the earth is full of your generosity, and the whole universe belongs to you. You are present everywhere, yet you chose to create life and give joy. You made me who I am, and everything I have has come from your hand. My life, my breath, my place in the world, and the limits of my days are all held by you. Thank you for ruling my life with wisdom, even when I do not understand what you are doing.
theological_themes: God is eternal, glorious, and present everywhere.
Creation displays God's glory and generosity.
Human life, location, gifts, and circumstances are dependent on God's providence.

scripture_references.connection: This psalm presents creation as a witness to God's glory, which supports the prayer's opening attention to the heavens and earth as displays of who God is.

Paul teaches that God made the world, gives life and breath to all, appoints people's times and places, and is the one in whom we live and move. This closely grounds the prayer's dependence on God for existence and circumstances.

sections.heading: Thanking you for showing me Jesus
sections.text: Thank you most of all for the riches you have given me in Jesus. Thank you that I am not left guessing who he is, because you have shown him clearly in Scripture. In your Word I see his glory, his mercy, his humility, his suffering, his death for sinners, and his resurrection. Keep opening my eyes to him, not as an idea I already understand, but as my living Savior, the one I need every day.
theological_themes: God's greatest gift is the revelation and saving work of Christ.
Scripture reveals Christ truly and clearly.
Jesus' incarnation, suffering, death, and resurrection are central to Christian faith.

scripture_references.connection: John explains that the written testimony about Jesus is given so that people may believe in him and have life in his name, which supports thanking God for revealing Christ in Scripture.
This passage traces Christ's humility, obedience, death, and exaltation, matching the prayer's focus on seeing Jesus' person, humiliation, suffering, and glory.

sections.heading: Admitting how much I still need mercy
sections.text: Please make me feel my need for Jesus not just once, but continually. Bring me low enough to tell the truth about myself. Like Job, I have no room to boast before you. Like Peter sinking in the water, I need you to save me. Like the tax collector in Jesus' story, my honest prayer is: God, have mercy on me, a sinner.
theological_themes: The believer remains dependent on Christ's ongoing saving help.
True prayer includes honest confession and humility before God.
Mercy is received by those who come to God without self-righteousness.

scripture_references.connection: This passage presents Jesus as the living intercessor who saves completely those who draw near to God through him, grounding the prayer's request to depend on his continual saving work.
Jesus commends the tax collector who pleads for mercy rather than trusting in his own righteousness, directly supporting the prayer's humble confession.
Peter's cry while sinking shows the urgency and simplicity of helpless dependence on Jesus, which the prayer uses as a model for personal need.

sections.heading: Asking for a changed heart, not only a cleared record
sections.text: Do not let me make peace with sin. Break the power of my love for it. I need forgiveness, but I also need to be remade. Cleanse me, and change what I desire, so that I can serve you with a freer heart and enjoy you forever.
theological_themes: Forgiveness and renewal belong together in God's saving work.
Sin is not only guilt to be pardoned but a power and desire to be subdued.
God changes his people so they can serve and enjoy him.

scripture_references.connection: God promises cleansing from uncleanness and the gift of a new heart and Spirit-led obedience, which grounds the prayer's distinction between forgiveness and inner renewal.
Paul calls believers to treat themselves as alive to God in Christ and not to let sin reign over them, supporting the request that the love and rule of sin be subdued.

sections.heading: Coming with nothing but Jesus
sections.text: I come to you in the name of Jesus. I have nothing impressive to bring you—no record of good works that could earn your welcome, no worthiness of my own, no promises I can make strong enough to secure your favor. I stray often. I knowingly resist your authority. I take your kindness and turn it into an excuse for myself. And because you have given me so much light—your Word, your gospel, your patience, your people—my guilt is heavier when I treat those gifts lightly or fail to use them well.
theological_themes: Access to God is through Christ, not personal merit.
Human righteousness cannot earn God's favor.
Greater spiritual privilege brings greater responsibility.

scripture_references.connection: Paul teaches that salvation is by grace through faith, not by works, which supports the prayer's refusal to plead personal merit before God.
Because Jesus is the great high priest, believers are invited to draw near to God for mercy and grace, grounding the prayer's approach to God in Jesus' name.
Jesus teaches that greater knowledge and entrusted responsibility increase accountability, which helps explain the prayer's concern that neglected spiritual privileges deepen guilt.

sections.heading: Wanting your favor and living before your face
sections.text: Yet, Father, I do care about your favor, and I do want your glory to matter more to me. Do not let me drift into coldness or carelessness. Press into my heart the truth that you are always near: when I go out, when I come home, when I work, when I rest, when I lie down, and when my life reaches its end. Let that awareness make me honest, watchful, comforted, and ready to live before you today.
theological_themes: God is omnipresent and personally aware of every part of life.
Remembering God's presence produces reverence, comfort, watchfulness, and faithfulness.
The believer desires God's favor and glory despite ongoing weakness.

scripture_references.connection: David confesses that God knows his sitting, rising, paths, words, and all places he could go, which grounds the prayer's closing request to live in awareness of God's constant presence.
Paul's aim to please the Lord in view of final accountability supports the prayer's desire to care about God's favor and live before him through all of life, including its end.

content_provenance.original_author: Unattributed Puritan source (compiled and edited by Arthur Bennett)
content_provenance.original_title: God the Source of All Good
content_provenance.original_source: The Valley of Vision: A Collection of Puritan Prayers and Devotions, ed. Arthur Bennett (The Banner of Truth Trust)
content_provenance.source_copyright_status: Compilation, titles and arrangement in copyright (Banner of Truth, 1975); underlying Puritan sources are public domain.
content_provenance.modern_version_note: Contemporary prayer based on the theological themes and ideas of the historical source; not a reproduction of the original wording.

theological_issues_identified: The original phrase 'continual saviourhood' could be misunderstood as implying Christ's atoning work is incomplete or repeatedly performed. The adaptation renders it as ongoing dependence on the living Savior and his intercession, while preserving the completed sufficiency of his saving work.

The original statement that 'much of my guilt arises from my religious privileges' reflects a Puritan concern that access to Scripture, gospel truth, and Christian nurture increases responsibility. This can sound harsh in modern ears, but it is biblically grounded and has been retained rather than softened.
significant_interpretive_choices: 'Renovation as well as forgiveness' was interpreted as inner renewal or sanctification, not merely moral self-improvement. The prayer therefore asks God to change desires and subdue the love of sin.

The three biblical cries in the original—Job's unworthiness, Peter's danger, and the publican's plea for mercy—were rendered as models of humility, helpless dependence, and repentance rather than as exact quotations from one English translation.

The closing line about God's presence around 'my path, my ways, my lying down, my end' was interpreted as a request to live consciously before God's omnipresent knowledge in ordinary life and in view of death/final accountability.
